title: Classes and objects: a second boat

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run the fleet here, and try your classes from main.

tasks.title: Write the Boat class
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `Fleet.java`, below the class with `main`, write a class called `Boat` with three fields: a `String` called `name`, an `int` called `seats` and an `int` called `aboard`, the people on board now. Give it a method `int seatsFree()` that gives back how many seats are free on this boat.

Check makes boats of its own with `new Boat()`, gives their fields values of its own, two boats at once included, and reads what `seatsFree()` gives back for each and what each boat's fields hold afterwards.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson about a class and its fields: a field is made like a variable, inside the class and outside any method.
Write the class's first line and its braces under the `// Task 1` comment, then the three fields.
Write `seatsFree` inside the class, without `static`, and work it out from the fields.
Take the `//` off the boat lines in `main` and run the file: the two boats should differ.
hints: The class goes below the closing brace of `Fleet`, not inside it. Its fields have a type and a name, and no value.
Inside `seatsFree`, `seats` and `aboard` mean the fields of the boat it was called on, so `linnet.seatsFree()` reads the Linnet's. A field with `static` in front would be one field for every boat.
The shape: `class Boat {`, then `String name;`, `int seats;`, `int aboard;`, then `int seatsFree() { return seats - aboard; }` and the closing brace.

tasks.title: Write the Ticket class, with a copy for the next passenger
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a class called `Ticket` with two fields, a `String` called `passenger` and an `int` called `pence`, and a method `Ticket copyFor(String who)`. It gives back a new ticket for `who` at the same fare, and leaves this ticket as it was.

Check makes tickets of its own, calls `copyFor`, reads the fields of both tickets, changes the copy, and reads the first ticket again.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson about two names for one object.
Write the class and its two fields.
In `copyFor`, make a new ticket and give each of its fields a value.
In `main`, print both tickets' passengers: they should differ.
hints: `Ticket other = this;` or giving back this ticket does not make a ticket: both names point at the one object. Only `new` makes a second one.
Make the new ticket with `new Ticket()`, then set its `passenger` to `who` and its `pence` to this ticket's `pence`.
Inside: `Ticket copy = new Ticket();`, then `copy.passenger = who;` and `copy.pence = pence;`, then `return copy;`.

tasks.title: Write the Crossing class, which may have no boat yet
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a class called `Crossing` with two fields, an `int` called `hour` and a `Boat` called `boat`, and a method `String boatName()`. It gives back the name of the crossing's boat, or `No boat` when the crossing has not been given a boat. It builds on Task 1.

Check makes crossings of its own, some with a boat and some without, two at once included, renames a boat after giving it to a crossing, and reads what `boatName()` gives back.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson about `null` and the exception it brings.
Write the class and its two fields; `Boat` is a type like `String`.
In `boatName`, handle a crossing without a boat first, before anything reads the boat.
Take the `//` off the crossing lines in `main` and run the file.
hints: A field of a class type that nobody set holds `null`: no boat at all. Reading `boat.name` then stops the program with a `NullPointerException`.
Ask whether the field is `null` with `==` before you read anything through it.
The shape: `if (boat == null) { return "No boat"; }`, then `return boat.name;`.
